subject: physics
topicDisplay: Unit 6: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: A motor turns a flywheel of rotational inertia I counterclockwise with angular speed ω. The motor is then reversed, and a short time later the flywheel turns clockwise with the same angular speed ω. Which claim about the flywheel's rotational kinetic energy is correct?
options: It is the same before and after, as rotational kinetic energy has no direction.
It changes sign, as a clockwise rotation gives the flywheel negative kinetic energy.
It increases by 2Iω², as the flywheel's angular velocity has changed by a total of 2ω.
It is greater after, as the motor has done work on the flywheel to reverse it.
optionWhy: K_rot = (1/2)Iω² depends on the square of the angular speed, which is the same before and after, and kinetic energy is a scalar with no direction. Reversing the sense of rotation does not change it.
A student who gives kinetic energy a sign set by the sense of rotation picks this. Kinetic energy is a scalar and is never negative; (1/2)Iω² is the same for either sense.
A student who finds the change in kinetic energy from the change in angular velocity picks this: (1/2)I(2ω)² = 2Iω². The kinetic energy before and after is (1/2)Iω² each time, so the change is zero.

A student who treats all work as adding energy picks this. While slowing the flywheel the motor does negative work on it, and while speeding it up again it does positive work; with the same final angular speed the total is zero.
questions.explain: K_rot = (1/2)Iω² depends on the square of the angular speed, which is the same before and after, and kinetic energy is a scalar with no direction. Reversing the sense of rotation does not change it.

questions.q: A uniform solid disk of mass 4.00 kg and radius 0.500 m rotates at 12.0 rad/s about a fixed axle through its center, perpendicular to its face. What is the rotational kinetic energy of the disk?
optionWhy: For a uniform solid disk about its central axis, I = (1/2)MR² = (1/2)(4.00 kg)(0.500 m)² = 0.500 kg·m². Then K_rot = (1/2)Iω² = (1/2)(0.500 kg·m²)(12.0 rad/s)² = 36.0 J.

A student who treats all of the disk's mass as if it were at the rim picks this: I = MR² = 1.00 kg·m² gives (1/2)(1.00)(12.0)² = 72.0 J. Much of a solid disk's mass is closer to the axle than R, so I = (1/2)MR².
A student who leaves out the square of the angular speed picks this: (1/2)(0.500)(12.0) = 3.00 J. Rotational kinetic energy is proportional to ω², so the angular speed must be squared.

A student who thinks an object whose center of mass is at rest has no kinetic energy picks this. The disk's center does not move, but every other point of the disk moves in a circle, so the disk has kinetic energy (1/2)Iω².
questions.explain: For a uniform solid disk about its central axis, I = (1/2)MR² = (1/2)(4.00 kg)(0.500 m)² = 0.500 kg·m². Then K_rot = (1/2)Iω² = (1/2)(0.500 kg·m²)(12.0 rad/s)² = 36.0 J.

questions.q: A thin uniform rod of mass M and length ℓ, whose rotational inertia about an axis through its center and perpendicular to it is (1/12)Mℓ², rotates about that axis with angular speed ω. The same rod is then made to rotate about a parallel axis through one end, with angular speed ω/2. What is the ratio of the rod's new rotational kinetic energy to its original rotational kinetic energy?
optionWhy: A student who uses the same rotational inertia about both axes picks this: only ω² changes, by a factor of 1/4. Rotational inertia depends on the axis; about the end it is (1/3)Mℓ², four times the value about the center.

A student who finds the rotational inertia correctly (four times as great) but takes kinetic energy to be proportional to ω picks this: 4 × 1/2 = 2.00. K_rot depends on ω², so halving ω divides the energy by 4.
About one end, the parallel axis theorem with d = ℓ/2 gives I = (1/12)Mℓ² + M(ℓ/2)² = (1/3)Mℓ², four times the value about the center. Halving ω multiplies ω² by 1/4. The ratio is 4 × 1/4 = 1.00.

A student who uses the rod's length as d in the parallel axis theorem picks this: I = (1/12)Mℓ² + Mℓ² = (13/12)Mℓ², 13 times the value about the center, and 13 × 1/4 = 3.25. The distance between the axes is ℓ/2, so I = (1/3)Mℓ².
questions.explain: About one end, the parallel axis theorem with d = ℓ/2 gives I = (1/12)Mℓ² + M(ℓ/2)² = (1/3)Mℓ², four times the value about the center. Halving ω multiplies ω² by 1/4. The ratio is 4 × 1/4 = 1.00.

questions.q: The diagram is a top view of a light rod that carries two small beads and rotates about a fixed vertical axle at the angular speed shown. The axle passes through the center of mass of the rod–bead system. What is the kinetic energy of the system?
optionWhy: A student who thinks a system whose center of mass is at rest has no kinetic energy picks this. The center of mass stays on the axle, but both beads move in circles, and each has kinetic energy (1/2)mv².

Each bead moves in a circle with v = rω: the 0.30 kg bead at (0.40 m)(5.0 rad/s) = 2.0 m/s and the 0.60 kg bead at (0.20 m)(5.0 rad/s) = 1.0 m/s. Their kinetic energies, 0.60 J and 0.30 J, add to 0.90 J, the same as (1/2)Iω² with I = 0.072 kg·m². The center of mass is at rest, but the beads are moving.

A student who thinks the beads' kinetic energies cancel because the beads move in opposite directions picks this: 0.60 J − 0.30 J = 0.30 J. Kinetic energy is a scalar and never negative, so the two values add.

A student who puts the system's whole mass at the far end of the rod picks this: I = (0.90 kg)(0.40 m)² = 0.144 kg·m² gives (1/2)(0.144)(5.0)² = 1.80 J. Each bead contributes mr² at its own distance from the axle.
questions.explain: Each bead moves in a circle with v = rω: the 0.30 kg bead at (0.40 m)(5.0 rad/s) = 2.0 m/s and the 0.60 kg bead at (0.20 m)(5.0 rad/s) = 1.0 m/s. Their kinetic energies, 0.60 J and 0.30 J, add to 0.90 J, the same as (1/2)Iω² with I = 0.072 kg·m². The center of mass is at rest, but the beads are moving.

questions.q: A mechanic pushes on a wrench, exerting a constant torque of 40 N·m on a rusted bolt for 5.0 s, but the bolt does not turn. Which statement about the energy the torque transfers to the bolt, with its reasoning, is correct?
options: Some energy, as the torque was exerted on the bolt for a time interval of 5.0 s.
None, as the rust exerts an equal and opposite torque that balances it.
None, as the bolt turned through no angle while the torque was exerted on it.
None, as the bolt's angular speed did not change during the 5.0 s.
optionWhy: A student who links the energy a torque transfers to how long it acts picks this. Work depends on the angular displacement, not the time: with no rotation the work is exactly zero, however long the torque acts.

A student who confuses the work done by one torque with the net work picks this. A balanced torque does work whenever the object turns, as a motor's torque does on a wheel turning steadily against friction; here it does none only because the bolt does not turn.
The work done by a torque is W = ∫τ dθ. The bolt did not rotate, so Δθ = 0 and the torque, however large and however long it is exerted, did no work on the bolt.

A student who thinks energy is transferred only when speed changes picks this. A motor turning a wheel at constant speed against friction transfers energy to it; what makes the work zero here is the zero angular displacement.
questions.explain: The work done by a torque is W = ∫τ dθ. The bolt did not rotate, so Δθ = 0 and the torque, however large and however long it is exerted, did no work on the bolt.
questions.working: W = ∫τ dθ = (40 N·m)(0 rad) = 0 J: no angular displacement, so no work, independent of the 5.0 s duration.

questions.q: A rope wound around a winch drum of radius 0.20 m is pulled with a constant force of magnitude 50 N, tangent to the drum, while the drum turns through 3.0 revolutions. How much work does the torque exerted by the rope do on the drum?
optionWhy: The torque is τ = rF = (0.20 m)(50 N) = 10 N·m, and the angular displacement is 3.0 rev × 2π rad/rev = 6.0π rad ≈ 18.8 rad. W = τΔθ = (10 N·m)(18.8 rad) ≈ 1.9 × 10² J. As a check, this equals the force times the length of rope pulled off, (50 N)(2π × 0.20 m × 3.0).
A student who uses the number of revolutions as the angular displacement picks this: (10 N·m)(3.0) = 30 J. W = τΔθ needs Δθ in radians, and 3.0 rev is 6.0π rad.
A student who leaves the lever arm out of the torque picks this: (50 N)(6.0π rad) ≈ 940 J. The torque of the rope is rF = 10 N·m, not 50 N·m.
A student who takes the torque itself, 10 N·m, as the energy transferred picks this. Torque and work share the unit N·m, but the work is the torque multiplied by the angular displacement, 6.0π rad.
questions.explain: The torque is τ = rF = (0.20 m)(50 N) = 10 N·m, and the angular displacement is 3.0 rev × 2π rad/rev = 6.0π rad ≈ 18.8 rad. W = τΔθ = (10 N·m)(18.8 rad) ≈ 1.9 × 10² J. As a check, this equals the force times the length of rope pulled off, (50 N)(2π × 0.20 m × 3.0).

questions.q: The graph shows the torque τ exerted on a wheel by a motor as a function of the wheel's angular position θ. How much work does this torque do on the wheel as the wheel turns from θ = 0 to θ = 6.0 rad?
optionWhy: A student who treats the torque as constant at its greatest value picks this: (6.0 N·m)(6.0 rad) = 36 J. The torque is less than 6.0 N·m everywhere except at θ = 2.0 rad, so the area under the graph is smaller.

A student who multiplies the torque at the final position by the whole angular displacement picks this: (4.0 N·m)(6.0 rad) = 24 J. The torque varies, so the work is the whole area under the graph, not one value times the width.

A student who averages the first and last torques, (0 + 4.0)/2 = 2.0 N·m, picks this: (2.0 N·m)(6.0 rad) = 12 J. The torque does not change linearly over the interval, so the mean of the end values is not its average; the area is 26 J.

The work is the area under the τ–θ graph. From 0 to 2.0 rad it is a triangle: (1/2)(2.0 rad)(6.0 N·m) = 6.0 J. From 2.0 to 6.0 rad it is a trapezoid: (1/2)(6.0 + 4.0 N·m)(4.0 rad) = 20 J. The total is 26 J.
questions.explain: The work is the area under the τ–θ graph. From 0 to 2.0 rad it is a triangle: (1/2)(2.0 rad)(6.0 N·m) = 6.0 J. From 2.0 to 6.0 rad it is a trapezoid: (1/2)(6.0 + 4.0 N·m)(4.0 rad) = 20 J. The total is 26 J.

questions.q: A constant net torque turns a wheel, initially at rest, through an angle θ₁; the wheel's angular speed is then ω₁. Starting again from rest, the same torque turns the same wheel through an angle 2θ₁. What is the wheel's new final angular speed divided by ω₁?
optionWhy: The work done by the constant torque is τΔθ, so doubling the angle doubles the work and the final kinetic energy, (1/2)Iω². Since ω ∝ √K, the angular speed increases by a factor of √2 ≈ 1.41.

A student who takes kinetic energy to be proportional to angular speed picks this: twice the work gives twice the angular speed. K_rot depends on ω², so twice the energy gives √2 times the angular speed.
A student who applies the dependence the wrong way round, squaring the factor instead of taking its square root, picks this: 2² = 4. Since ω² ∝ W, the factor for ω is √2.

A student who thinks a given torque produces a given angular speed picks this. A net torque produces angular acceleration, so the longer it acts (here, through twice the angle) the faster the wheel turns.
questions.explain: The work done by the constant torque is τΔθ, so doubling the angle doubles the work and the final kinetic energy, (1/2)Iω². Since ω ∝ √K, the angular speed increases by a factor of √2 ≈ 1.41.
questions.working: W = τΔθ; (1/2)Iω² = τΔθ → ω ∝ √Δθ. Doubling Δθ: ω/ω₁ = √2 = 1.41.

questions.q: The diagram shows a wheel rotating counterclockwise on a fixed axle. For a short time interval, while the wheel is still rotating counterclockwise, a force F⃗ tangent to the rim is exerted on the wheel at the point shown. Which describes the angular impulse about the axle that this force delivers to the wheel?
options: Counterclockwise, the same sense as the wheel's rotation during the interval
It has no sense, as an angular impulse has a size but no direction
To the right, along the force, like the linear impulse of the force
Clockwise, the same sense as the torque the force exerts about the axle
optionWhy: A student who thinks an impulse acts in the direction of the motion picks this. The angular impulse has the sense of the torque, which is clockwise here; it opposes the rotation and slows the wheel.
A student who treats angular impulse as a plain amount picks this. Angular impulse has the direction of the torque that delivers it; here it is clockwise.
A student who carries over the direction rule for linear impulse picks this. The force's linear impulse is to the right, but its angular impulse about the axle has the sense of its torque: clockwise.

At the top of the rim, a force to the right turns the wheel clockwise about the axle, so its torque is clockwise. Angular impulse has the direction of the torque that delivers it, so it is clockwise, opposite to the wheel's rotation, and it reduces the wheel's angular momentum.
questions.explain: At the top of the rim, a force to the right turns the wheel clockwise about the axle, so its torque is clockwise. Angular impulse has the direction of the torque that delivers it, so it is clockwise, opposite to the wheel's rotation, and it reduces the wheel's angular momentum.

questions.q: Two identical wheels, A and B, are at rest on fixed, frictionless axles. A net torque of 8.0 N·m is exerted on wheel A for 0.50 s, and a net torque of 2.0 N·m is exerted on wheel B for 2.0 s. How do the wheels' angular momenta compare after the torques have ended?
options: Wheel A's is greater, as the torque on wheel A is greater
Wheel B's is greater, as the torque on wheel B acts for longer
Equal, as the two wheels receive equal angular impulses
Equal only if the two wheels turn through equal angles
optionWhy: A student who judges the effect by the size of the torque alone picks this. The torque on B is smaller but acts four times as long, so the angular impulses, and the changes in angular momentum, are equal.
A student who judges the effect by the duration alone picks this. The torque on A acts for a quarter of the time but is four times as large, so the angular impulses are equal.

Each wheel receives an angular impulse τΔt = 4.0 N·m·s (8.0 × 0.50 and 2.0 × 2.0). The angular impulse equals the change in angular momentum, and both wheels start from rest, so they end with equal angular momenta.
A student who links the change in angular momentum to the angle turned, as for work, picks this. The angular impulse is ∫τ dt over time; it does not depend on the angle through which the wheel turns.
questions.explain: Each wheel receives an angular impulse τΔt = 4.0 N·m·s (8.0 × 0.50 and 2.0 × 2.0). The angular impulse equals the change in angular momentum, and both wheels start from rest, so they end with equal angular momenta.
questions.working: A: (8.0 N·m)(0.50 s) = 4.0 N·m·s. B: (2.0 N·m)(2.0 s) = 4.0 N·m·s. ΔL equal; both start from rest, so L_A = L_B.

questions.q: A wheel turns on a fixed axle. Which statement correctly relates the net torque exerted on the wheel to the wheel's angular momentum about the axle?
options: The net torque is proportional to the angular momentum that the wheel has.
The net torque is zero at any instant when the wheel's angular momentum is zero.
A net torque is needed to keep any nonzero angular momentum going.
The net torque sets how fast the angular momentum changes, not its value.
optionWhy: A student who links torque to the rotation itself rather than to its change picks this. A wheel turning steadily on a frictionless axle has angular momentum but zero net torque.
A student who thinks zero angular momentum means zero torque picks this. A wheel reversing its rotation has L = 0 for an instant while a net torque is still changing its angular momentum.
A student who thinks rotation needs a continuing torque picks this. With zero net torque, the angular momentum does not change; a net torque is needed only to change it.

Newton's second law in rotational form is τ_net = dL/dt: the net torque is the rate of change of the angular momentum, which for constant rotational inertia is Iα. The angular momentum itself can have any value when the net torque is zero.
questions.explain: Newton's second law in rotational form is τ_net = dL/dt: the net torque is the rate of change of the angular momentum, which for constant rotational inertia is Iα. The angular momentum itself can have any value when the net torque is zero.

questions.q: Wheel A, with rotational inertia I, spins at angular speed 2ω on a fixed axle with negligible friction. Wheel B, with rotational inertia 2I, spins at angular speed ω in the opposite sense on the same axle, without touching wheel A. Which statement about the total angular momentum of the two-wheel system about the axle is correct?
options: It is 4Iω, as each wheel contributes 2Iω and the two contributions add
It is in wheel A's sense, as wheel A has the greater angular speed
It is zero, as the wheels' angular momenta are equal and opposite
It is in wheel B's sense, as wheel B has the greater rotational inertia
optionWhy: A student who adds magnitudes regardless of sense picks this. Each wheel does have 2Iω, but they turn in opposite senses, so one is positive and the other negative and they cancel.

A student who judges angular momentum by angular speed alone picks this. Wheel A spins twice as fast, but wheel B has twice the rotational inertia, so their values of Iω are equal and the total is zero.

The total is the sum of the parts' angular momenta about the axle, with signs. Wheel A has I(2ω) = 2Iω in one sense and wheel B has (2I)ω = 2Iω in the other, so they cancel and the total is zero (although each wheel has kinetic energy).

A student who judges angular momentum by rotational inertia alone picks this. Wheel B has twice the rotational inertia, but it spins at half the angular speed, so its Iω equals wheel A's and the total is zero.
questions.explain: The total is the sum of the parts' angular momenta about the axle, with signs. Wheel A has I(2ω) = 2Iω in one sense and wheel B has (2I)ω = 2Iω in the other, so they cancel and the total is zero (although each wheel has kinetic energy).
questions.working: Take wheel A's sense as positive: L_A = I(2ω) = +2Iω and L_B = (2I)(−ω) = −2Iω. Total = 0.

questions.q: A space station floats far from other objects. A motor mounted on the station spins up a flywheel whose rotational inertia is much smaller than the station's, about an axis shared with the station. During the spin-up, how does the angular impulse exerted on the flywheel by the station compare with the angular impulse exerted on the station by the flywheel?
options: Larger on the flywheel, as the station is far more massive than the flywheel
Larger on the station, as the flywheel ends up spinning faster than the station
Zero on the station, as the motor turns only the flywheel, not the station
Equal in size and opposite in sense, as the two torques form a third-law pair
optionWhy: A student who thinks the larger body exerts the larger torque picks this. The torques the two exert on each other form a third-law pair, equal and opposite whatever their sizes, so the angular impulses are equal in magnitude.

A student who thinks the faster-spinning object exerts the larger torque picks this. The flywheel's larger angular speed comes from its smaller rotational inertia (Δω = ΔL/I), not from a larger angular impulse; the two angular impulses are equal and opposite.

A student who thinks only the active agent exerts a torque picks this. The flywheel exerts an equal and opposite torque back on the motor and so on the station, which therefore starts to turn the other way.

The station (through the motor) and the flywheel exert torques on each other about the shared axis. By Newton's third law these torques are equal in magnitude and opposite in sense at every instant, so the angular impulses are too. The flywheel ends up spinning faster only because its rotational inertia is smaller.
questions.explain: The station (through the motor) and the flywheel exert torques on each other about the shared axis. By Newton's third law these torques are equal in magnitude and opposite in sense at every instant, so the angular impulses are too. The flywheel ends up spinning faster only because its rotational inertia is smaller.

questions.q: A flywheel spins on an axle mounted in a machine frame that is bolted to the floor. A brake pad fixed to the frame presses on the flywheel and brings it to rest. Which statement about the angular momentum that the flywheel loses is correct?
options: It turns into thermal energy in the pad and wheel
It runs down, as the spin of every object does in time
It is passed through the frame and the floor to Earth
It is destroyed, as friction is a nonconservative force
optionWhy: A student who conflates angular momentum with energy picks this. The flywheel's kinetic energy becomes thermal energy, but angular momentum is a different quantity and cannot become energy; it is transferred to Earth.

A student who thinks spin dies away by itself picks this. The flywheel slows because the brake exerts a torque on it; without that torque it would keep spinning, and the angular momentum it loses goes to Earth.

Angular momentum is conserved in all interactions. The pad exerts a torque on the flywheel, and the flywheel exerts an equal and opposite torque on the pad, frame and floor, so Earth gains the angular momentum the flywheel loses. Earth's enormous rotational inertia means its rotation changes immeasurably.

A student who reads 'nonconservative' as 'does not conserve' picks this. That word describes the path dependence of a force's work; angular momentum is conserved in every interaction, including frictional ones, and passes to Earth.
questions.explain: Angular momentum is conserved in all interactions. The pad exerts a torque on the flywheel, and the flywheel exerts an equal and opposite torque on the pad, frame and floor, so Earth gains the angular momentum the flywheel loses. Earth's enormous rotational inertia means its rotation changes immeasurably.

questions.q: The diagram shows a wheel rolling without slipping to the right along level ground; the velocity of its center C is v. Points P and Q are on the rim at the positions shown. Which statement about the speeds of P and Q relative to the ground at this instant is correct?
options: P and Q both move forward at speed v, as C does
P moves at speed 2v, and Q is momentarily at rest
P moves forward and Q moves backward, each at speed v
P and Q both move at speed 2v, twice that of C
optionWhy: A student who treats the wheel as moving along without turning gives every point the center's speed. The rotation adds a velocity of magnitude v forward at the top and backward at the bottom, so P moves at 2v and Q is at rest.

Each point moves with the center's velocity v plus its velocity from rotation, of magnitude Rω = v. At the top, P, both point forward and add to 2v; at the contact point, Q, the rotational velocity points backward and cancels v, as rolling without slipping requires.
A student who considers only the wheel's rotation about its center picks this; it describes the motion relative to the center. Adding the center's velocity v gives 2v for P and zero for Q.

A student who adds the speeds from translation and rotation as numbers gets v + v at both points. They must be added as vectors: they point the same way at P but opposite ways at Q, which is instantaneously at rest.
questions.explain: Each point moves with the center's velocity v plus its velocity from rotation, of magnitude Rω = v. At the top, P, both point forward and add to 2v; at the contact point, Q, the rotational velocity points backward and cancels v, as rolling without slipping requires.
questions.working: v_P = v + Rω = 2v (forward); v_Q = v − Rω = 0, since v = Rω.

questions.q: A uniform solid ball rolls without slipping down a rough incline. Air resistance is negligible, and the ball and the incline are rigid. The coefficient of static friction between them is μ_s, and the normal force on the ball is F_N. Which statement about the friction force exerted on the ball by the incline is correct?
options: It acts on a point that is momentarily at rest, so it dissipates no energy
It is zero, because the ball does not slide along the surface of the incline
It equals μ_sF_N, because static friction is what keeps the ball from slipping
It converts some of the ball's mechanical energy into thermal energy as it rolls
optionWhy: For rolling without slipping the contact point has no velocity relative to the incline, so the static friction force acting there does no work and dissipates no energy. It is not zero: it exerts the torque about the center that gives the ball its angular acceleration.

A student who links friction only with sliding picks this. Static friction acts at the contact point; without it there would be no torque about the center, and the ball would slide down without starting to turn.

A student who takes static friction to be μ_sF_N picks this. μ_sF_N is the largest value static friction can have; the actual value is whatever rolling without slipping needs, (2/7)Mg sin θ for a uniform ball.
A student who thinks every friction force dissipates energy picks this. The contact point does not slide, so friction does no work, and the ball's mechanical energy is constant.
questions.explain: For rolling without slipping the contact point has no velocity relative to the incline, so the static friction force acting there does no work and dissipates no energy. It is not zero: it exerts the torque about the center that gives the ball its angular acceleration.

questions.q: A uniform solid cylinder rolls without slipping across a level floor with total kinetic energy K. A thin hoop with the same mass and the same radius rolls without slipping across the floor at the same speed. What is the total kinetic energy of the hoop?
optionWhy: Each total is translational plus rotational kinetic energy, with ω = v/R. The cylinder has (1/2)Mv² + (1/4)Mv² = (3/4)Mv² = K; the hoop has (1/2)Mv² + (1/2)Mv² = Mv². So the hoop's total is K/(3/4) = 1.33K.

A student who gives every round object the rotational inertia MR² treats the cylinder like the hoop and finds equal totals. A uniform solid cylinder has I = (1/2)MR², so less of its energy is rotational.

A student who adds the rotational kinetic energy about the contact point to the translational energy finds (1/2 + 3/4)Mv² for the cylinder and (1/2 + 1)Mv² for the hoop, a ratio of 1.20. Rotation about the contact point already includes the translation; use the rotational inertia about the center.

A student who takes total kinetic energy to be proportional to rotational inertia doubles K because the hoop's I is twice the cylinder's. Only the rotational part doubles; the translational part, (1/2)Mv², is the same for both, so the ratio is 4/3.
questions.explain: Each total is translational plus rotational kinetic energy, with ω = v/R. The cylinder has (1/2)Mv² + (1/4)Mv² = (3/4)Mv² = K; the hoop has (1/2)Mv² + (1/2)Mv² = Mv². So the hoop's total is K/(3/4) = 1.33K.
questions.working: With v = Rω: cylinder K = (1/2)Mv² + (1/2)(1/2)MR²(v/R)² = (3/4)Mv². Hoop: (1/2)Mv² + (1/2)MR²(v/R)² = Mv². Ratio = 1/(3/4) = 4/3, so K_hoop = 1.33K.

questions.q: A small satellite orbits a planet whose mass is about 10²⁰ times the satellite's mass. In analyzing the orbit, the planet is treated as stationary. Which statement correctly justifies this?
options: Each exerts an equal force on the other, but the planet's acceleration is tiny.
The planet pulls on the satellite much harder than the satellite pulls on it.
The satellite's mass is far too small for it to exert a gravitational force at all.
In orbit the satellite is weightless, so the two of them exert no forces on each other.
optionWhy: The gravitational forces the satellite and planet exert on each other are a Newton's third-law pair, equal in magnitude. By Newton's second law the planet's acceleration is that force divided by its mass, about 10²⁰ times smaller than the satellite's, so its motion is negligible.
A student who thinks the more massive object exerts the larger force picks this. The two forces are a third-law pair and have equal magnitudes; the difference is in the accelerations they produce.
A student who thinks only massive bodies exert gravitational forces picks this. The satellite pulls on the planet with a force equal in magnitude to the planet's pull on it, G Mm/r².

A student who thinks there is no gravity in orbit picks this. Gravity is the force that keeps the satellite in orbit; the satellite is only apparently weightless, because gravity is the only force on it.
questions.explain: The gravitational forces the satellite and planet exert on each other are a Newton's third-law pair, equal in magnitude. By Newton's second law the planet's acceleration is that force divided by its mass, about 10²⁰ times smaller than the satellite's, so its motion is negligible.

questions.q: The diagram shows a satellite's elliptical orbit around a planet, with two points of the orbit marked P and A. The only force on the satellite is the planet's gravity. Which quantity is greater when the satellite is at P than when it is at A?
options: the system's total mechanical energy
the satellite's angular momentum
the system's potential energy U_g
the kinetic energy of the satellite
optionWhy: A student who equates the system's total energy with the satellite's kinetic energy picks this. With only gravitational forces between the two objects, the total mechanical energy is the same at P and A; the larger K at P is balanced by a lower U_g.

A student who thinks angular momentum increases with speed picks this. The satellite's angular momentum about the planet is constant; at P its larger speed is matched by its smaller distance, so rv is the same at P and A.
A student who compares the sizes of the negative values picks this, since |U_g| is larger at P. U_g = −GMm/r is more negative, so smaller, at P; it is greater at A, farther from the planet.

P is much closer to the planet than A. The system's mechanical energy is constant, and U_g = −GMm/r is lower (more negative) at P, so K is greater at P: the satellite moves fastest at its closest point.
questions.explain: P is much closer to the planet than A. The system's mechanical energy is constant, and U_g = −GMm/r is lower (more negative) at P, so K is greater at P: the satellite moves fastest at its closest point.

questions.q: A satellite is at distance r from the center of a planet of radius R. The gravitational potential energy U of the satellite–planet system is defined to be zero when r is infinite. Which graph shows U as a function of r for r ≥ R?
options: Graph 1
Graph 2
Graph 3
Graph 4
optionWhy: A student who writes the potential energy as +GMm/r picks the positive curve falling toward zero. With zero at infinity, U = −GMm/r is negative at every finite distance.

A student who uses U = mgΔy at every distance picks the straight line rising from zero at the surface. That treats the field as constant and puts the zero at the surface; for a satellite system U = −GMm/r, which levels off toward zero.
U = −GMm/r is negative for every finite r, has its lowest value, −GMm/R, at the surface, and rises toward zero as r increases, more and more slowly because its slope GMm/r² decreases.

A student who keeps the zero of potential energy at the planet's surface picks the curve rising from zero at R. That curve, GMm(1/R − 1/r), has the right shape but the wrong zero: the stem defines U = 0 at infinite separation.
questions.explain: U = −GMm/r is negative for every finite r, has its lowest value, −GMm/R, at the surface, and rises toward zero as r increases, more and more slowly because its slope GMm/r² decreases.
questions.working: U = −GMm/r: negative at every finite r, equal to −GMm/R at the surface, and increasing toward zero (from below) as r increases, with slope GMm/r² that decreases with r.

figure.alt: Four graphs, numbered 1 to 4, each of U (vertical axis, positive upward, with the r axis across the middle) against r (horizontal axis), with R marked on the r axis; each curve is drawn for r ≥ R. Panel 1: the curve starts at a positive value at R and falls, ever less steeply, toward zero, staying above the r axis. Panel 2: a straight line that starts at zero at R and rises steadily. Panel 3: the curve starts at a negative value at R and rises, ever less steeply, toward zero, staying below the r axis. Panel 4: the curve starts at zero at R and rises, ever less steeply, toward a positive value.
